text: Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. Every province collects a bad harvest this year." Population holds at three hundred million, times three, so read the x3 row of your tables and the bad-harvest column. No personal disasters on this card. Rich, a lean year makes a Land Deed worth more to the man selling it than to the one keeping it in a cupboard. Let's have that polite conversation before the auction.
Rich pays out a bad harvest at x3. Last year's new land pays for the first time: Reina +10, Graham +50, Rich +10, Clark +90, Noah +70, Paddy +30; Silke -10 and Rob -40, paid into the Pile.

The harvest, friends, every grain counted in front of witnesses: Clark ninety, Noah seventy, Paddy thirty, Graham fifty, our gracious Empress ten, and ten for your humble landlord. Silke and Rob, ten and forty into the Pile, if you please, and thank you. Rent's five, same as it was when I first held this purse, because a lean year is no time to squeeze the people who grow the rice. And Silke, I'd love to have that conversation. You're quite right that a lean year makes the Deed worth more to the man selling it, and that's exactly why the price isn't going down.
Rents: Rich keeps the rent at 5; Clark, Noah and Paddy each pay him 5.

A rotten harvest is no year to squeeze anyone, so it's twenty percent, the lowest the law allows, and Graham, the crown is building your irrigation out of its own purse, all thirty of it. And every new square anyone buys this year, the treasury pays in full. Nobody at this table will have a revolt clause to wave at me, darling. Not one.
If the last work owed is built, the game ends at once, in the public works step (Section 18): no auction, march or salaries follow it.

The tax is collected. Clark eighteen, Noah fourteen, Paddy six, Rich two, and ten from me, fifty in all. I'll count it again in front of you before it goes to the Empress, and Rob, I've written down that you refused. Majesty, I accept the irrigation at thirty, and I'll take all six squares you're offering in full: E11 to E15 and F10. That's a hundred and twenty out of the crown's purse. You said "every square, in full," and I've written it down in those exact words.
Rob owed no tax this year: his harvest income was -40.

Graham collects the 20% tax, 50 in all (Graham 10, Rich 2, Clark 18, Noah 14, Paddy 6). He agrees to the Province 2 Irrigation System at the crown's cost of 30, and buys six squares of new land for Province 2, E11-E15 and F10, the crown paying all 120.
F18 and F19 are Province 1's own squares, not new land, so they can't be bought; new land for Province 1 is listed below.

Graham darling, "every square, in full" is in the minutes and the crown pays it, all hundred and twenty, without a murmur. I'll keep my own fields as they are, though. An Empress who's just paid off the last of the realm's works doesn't need to dig up the north-east to prove anything.
Reina buys no new land for Province 1.

Majesty, I've never heard a more generous sentence from a throne, and I sat on one for six years. 'Every new square anyone buys this year, the treasury pays in full.' I'll take the only square I'm offered, F9, and the crown pays all twenty. Graham's written your words down, and I'm glad to be in his minutes for once.
Rich buys F9 for Province 3; the crown pays all 20.

Storyteller's tip: the game ends the moment the last work owed is built, in the public works step, so if the Irrigation System goes up this year no auction follows it (Section 18). A set can also be completed by a private trade at any time (Section 5).

Majesty, I'm holding you to it as well: "every new square, in full." Three squares on my coast, I25, I26 and J26, sixty grain from the treasury, and Graham can put me in the minutes next to Rich. It's a lean year, so a scholar takes what's offered.

Sixty-five grain for one Land Deed, handed over now, before the irrigation goes up. You said a lean year doesn't bring the price down, so I'm not asking it to. That's more than Noah will offer you in public, and with no auction coming it's the last sale you'll ever make. Say yes and the grain is yours this minute.
Silke buys I25, I26 and J26 for Province 4; the crown pays all 60.

Majesty, "every new square anyone buys this year, the treasury pays in full," and Graham's already got it written down word for word, so I'll take the whole ring: J27 to L27, M27 and M28, N28, O28, P28, and Q26 to Q28. Eleven squares, two hundred and twenty from the crown. And for the minutes, that's the first entry I've ever filed under "Reina, generous".
Clark buys eleven squares of sea for Province 5 (J27, K27, L27, M27, M28, N28, O28, P28, Q26-Q28); the crown pays all 220, and its reserve is down to 104.

Majesty, I'll be honest about it, since someone ought to be: Clark's ring has left the treasury on a hundred and four, and five squares is a hundred. So I'll take five, U24 to U26, T27 and S27, all at the crown's cost, 'every square, in full', and that leaves you four grain and your good name. I'm not asking for a sixth. I can count, and the purse can't pay for it.
Noah buys five squares for Province 6 (U24-U26, T27, S27); the crown pays all 100. The crown's reserve is down to 4; the Irrigation System it promised costs 30.

Majesty, I'd hold you to it too if there was anything left to hold, but I can count as well as Noah and four grain won't dig a ditch. I'll keep my own purse shut and keep my fields as they are. Graham, put me down in the minutes as the one who didn't ask.
Paddy buys no new land for Province 7.
Silke's whispered offer for a Deed can't be taken up: a seller's unsold stock is sold only at auction, never by private trade (Section 10).

Well. The treasury's down to four grain and a promise, so I'll keep my own purse shut on land, thank you, Majesty. Rob, I've paid you for the view every year since Year 2. I'd like to buy something from you for once.

Seventy-two grain for the Deed on E8, now, quietly. That's every grain I can spare and keep my claim, and it's more than that Deed has ever been worth to you in the desert. Noah has the purse to bid against me in public, so say yes before he works out what's going on.

Silke, my dear, I've had a few kind offers in my time, and that's among the kindest. But nothing on my mantel is for sale. The desert doesn't sell, it collects. And from where I'm standing, your front garden looks well stocked already.

Well, darling, I said every square in full and I meant it, and you've all held me to it beautifully: four hundred grain of new fields, every one in somebody else's province. Graham, the irrigation is in your fields, the crown has just put a hundred and twenty into your new land, and the crown has four grain left. Put in twenty-six and you'll have a ditch out of it, plus the honour of signing the last entry in your own minutes.
The crown paid 520 for new land this year (Graham 120, Rich 20, Silke 60, Clark 220, Noah 100), not four hundred.

Majesty, the minutes say "the crown paying all thirty," and they're your words, not mine. I won't pay twenty-six to close the book on a page where I hold nothing. The ditch can wait until the treasury can pay for it. Rob refused his tax and I've recorded that, so I'll record that the crown's ditch is still owed as well.

Public works: nothing is built in Year 13. The crown has 4, the Province 2 Irrigation System costs 30, and Graham won't pay toward it. 30 of the works are still owed, and the year goes on to the auction.
I'm starting from zero again, so the figures are small and honest, one for each piece. Silke, you need one Deed, and everyone here can count to one. I'm not going to make it cheap for you.

Friends, a landlord with forty-eight grain can't start a war, so I'll be bidding a grain over and never two, as usual. The Deed opens at sixty-five. A lean year doesn't lower the price, and I've heard there's at least one scholar at this table who agrees with me. If she meant it, she can say it again in the auction where everyone can hear.

You all know what I'm after, so I won't pretend otherwise: one Deed, and everything else can go where it likes. Noah, you'd need the Jar as well as the Deed, and Rich has two more Deeds for next year. Stand aside on this one, and when I'm in the chair your fields get the first works the crown builds. Graham can write that down too.

For the minutes: I'm in for the Customs House, the Deed and the Bowl, and out of the Brush and the Vase, so Graham and Rich can sort those out between them. Silke, the Deed's your last piece and I know it, so I'm not starting a war over it. My Jar opens at ten, and anyone who wants it pays for the privilege, same as I did.

Here's the sum out loud, since that's my job at this table. I need the Deed and the Jar and twenty to sit down with. Silke needs only the Deed, and on ninety-two and a half she can write seventy-two and still keep her twenty. So I'm writing more than that for Rich's Deed, and whatever's left goes on Clark's Jar. Rich, I'd sooner settle it fair than feed the Pile, but I won't stand aside, not on this one. And my Bowl goes up at five. Somebody ought to own it.

I've fifty-two and a half grain and three holes in my set, so I'll not pretend I'm the big money today. But I've come second by one grain too many times, so I'll be in on the Customs House, the Deed and the Jar for as long as my purse lets me. And my Vase is up at two, for anyone who wants a good pot cheap.
Thirteen years and not a single lot, friends, and I see no reason to break the habit now. Bid away. The desert's just here for the show.

The auction, settled from the limits: Graham's Customs House to Clark for 19 (Paddy out at 18); Rich's Land Deed Scroll to Noah for 73 (Silke out at 72); Silke's Bamboo Brush to Graham for 10; Clark's Dragon Jar to Noah for 17 (Graham and Paddy out at 16).

Silke, I'm sorry, and I mean that. You offered me the first works if I stood aside, and I told you plainly I wouldn't. Here's the sum, out loud like always: fifty-five and a half of mine plus your ninety-five is a hundred and fifty and a half, and the Scholar's chair. I read the cards for this table in Year One, and I'll read them honestly again. Clark, you need only a Deed now and Rich has two left, so I know whose chair I'm sitting in, and I'll be watching you.

Noah shows the Rice Peasant's set and replaces Silke as the Scholar, taking her 95 (150.5 in all); his Customs House, Vase, Deed and Jar go to J22, K22, M22 and M23 in Province 4, and his Brush joins Province 4's stock. Silke's pieces go back to stock; she draws 60 and is the Rice Peasant. Then Noah's old Wooden Bowl (now Silke's to sell) goes to Clark for 19 (Graham out at 18), and Paddy's Vase to Graham for 9 (Rich out at 8). Clark now needs only a Land Deed.

Customs House on P25 and the Bowl on O26, both down on the coast beside the Brush and well out of any soldier's walk. Paddy, out at eighteen this time, and it's my turn to say "by one", but I won't write it on your page. Noah, you're right to watch me. Rich has two Deeds left, and I'll be on the far side of the table when they come up.

A Brush for ten and a Vase for nine. That's nineteen grain for two pieces, after years of paying fifty for one. They'll go at the back of the G column, where nobody's boots reach. Silke, I'm sorry. I said I wouldn't make the Deed cheap for you, and I didn't need to, because Noah made it dear.
Clark puts the Customs House on P25 and the Bowl on O26; Graham puts the Brush on G12 and the Vase on G13.
Correction to the march menu's distance list: Noah's Vase (K22) is 2 rounds from W5, not 3.

Clark, you said the coast was well out of any soldier's walk. W4 has always been a keen walker. I'll look after your Vase on M18, and you can pop by and see it whenever you like. Graham, a little something from your fields as well, and Majesty, my lad's knocking at the north-east door, so do have a look in the cushions.

Rob marches: W1 onto I12 (Graham pays 5); W2 to J15; W3 onto I19 in Province 1 (Reina owes 10 with 4 in the reserve, so the crown goes 6 into debt to the Pile); W4 onto L25, taking Clark's Vase to M18 on the desert; W5 onto L19 (Noah pays 5).

Salaries: Reina pays what she declared, 8 to Graham and 8 to Noah; with no realia to sell, the crown's debt to the Pile is now 22. End of Year 13: Rob 198.5, Noah 153.5, Graham 86.5, Clark 66.5, Rich 66.5, Silke 64.5, Paddy 54.5, Reina -22 (in debt). Works owed: 30, the Province 2 Irrigation System. Clark needs a Land Deed and a Vase; Graham a Deed, a Jar and a Bowl. A player in debt is a cause for revolt (Section 16).
